For an electric-dipole transition,
\[
\Delta l=\pm1,\qquad \Delta m=0,\pm1.
\]

Thus the intermediate state must be \(2p\):
\[
|3,0,0\rangle\rightarrow |2,1,m'\rangle\rightarrow |1,0,0\rangle,
\qquad m'=-1,0,1.
\]

For the first transition, the Wigner–Eckart theorem gives
\[
\left\langle 2,1,m'\left|r_q\right|3,0,0\right\rangle
\propto \delta_{q,m'},
\]
with the same magnitude for all three values \(m'=-1,0,1\). The radial integral and transition frequency are also identical because the \(2p\) magnetic sublevels are degenerate. Therefore,
\[
P(3s\rightarrow 2p,m')=\frac13
\]
for each \(m'\).

Each \(2p\) sublevel subsequently decays to \(|1,0,0\rangle\) with unit branching probability. Hence
\[
P\!\left(|3,0,0\rangle\rightarrow |2,1,0\rangle
\rightarrow |1,0,0\rangle\right)
=\frac13.
\]
The three intermediate-\(m'\) routes each have probability \(1/3\), so their total is \(1\); no additional factor of \(2\) should be introduced.

Answer: D
